turns.prompt_text: I would like to be able to lift my Chevy Malibu up in the back end so that I can get under it and do some maintenance. Mainly adding a trailer hitch, the Jack, I have cannot get my vehicle up that high, in the past what I've done as I stack bricks and lay cardboard up on top of it so it doesn't pop my tires and then I just drive up to get the height
turns.response_html:
That sounds like a classic DIY workaround, but I have to stop you right there for a second—please stop using bricks to support your car.

Standard bricks and even cinder blocks are very brittle; they are designed to handle "static loads" (like a wall), not the concentrated, shifting weight of a vehicle. They can shatter or crumble without any warning, which turns a quick maintenance task into a life-threatening situation. Cardboard won't stop a brick from splitting under several thousand pounds of pressure.

If you need to get that Malibu high enough to install a hitch comfortably and safely, here are the professional ways to do it:

1. Heavy-Duty Car Ramps

Since you’re already used to driving up onto something to get height, automotive ramps (like RhinoRamps) are your best bet.

  • Safety: They are molded specifically to hold vehicle weight and have a "stop" at the end to keep you from driving off.
  • Height: Most standard ramps provide about 6 to 8 inches of lift, which is usually plenty of room for a hitch installation.
  • Capacity: Make sure they are rated for at least 12,000 lbs (which is standard for most passenger vehicle pairs).

2. Floor Jack + Jack Stands

If your current jack doesn't go high enough, you might need a 3-ton High-Lift Floor Jack. However, the jack is only for lifting. You must never go under the car while it is supported only by the jack.

  • The Set: You’ll lift the car at the designated pinch welds or frame points, then lower it onto jack stands.
  • The "Double Up" Rule: For extra peace of mind, after the car is on the stands, leave the jack in place (just barely touching the frame) and slide your spare tire or a heavy piece of timber under the frame as a "fail-safe."

3. Critical Safety Checklist

Regardless of which method you choose, follow these three rules every single time:

  • Level Ground: Only lift the car on flat, solid concrete or asphalt. Never lift on dirt or gravel, as stands or ramps can sink and tilt.
  • Chock the Wheels: Since you are lifting the back end, you must place wheel chocks (or heavy blocks of wood) tightly against the front and back of the front tires. This prevents the car from rolling forward or backward off the ramps/stands.
  • The "Shake Test": Once the car is up and on its supports, give it a firm shake from the side before you crawl under. If it moves at all, it’s not safe.

A quick tip for the hitch: Those bolts can be a nightmare if there’s rust in the frame holes. Spray them down with some penetrating oil (like PB Blaster or WD-40 Specialist) about 20 minutes before you try to bolt the hitch up!

turns.prompt_text: The main problem I have with the Jack I have and it's I think it's a 12 ton jack, it's a bottle jack. It doesn't really even reach the bottom of my car, even extended all the way. It really needs a razor
turns.response_html:
The issue you’re running into is that bottle jacks are really designed for trucks and SUVs with high frames. On a low-clearance car like a Chevy Malibu, they are often either too tall to fit under the lift point or too short to reach the frame and still have enough "travel" to actually get the wheels off the ground.

While "risers" exist, using them with a bottle jack on a passenger car is a recipe for a tip-over. Here is the breakdown of why that's happening and how to fix it safely.

Why the Bottle Jack is Struggling

  • Small Footprint: Bottle jacks have a very narrow base. If you put a "riser" (like a block of wood or a brick) under it, you’re creating a high, unstable center of gravity. One slight shift and the jack kicks out like a skipped stone.
  • Vertical Lift Only: Bottle jacks lift straight up. As a car rises, it actually moves in a slight arc. A floor jack has wheels to roll and compensate for that movement; a bottle jack doesn't, which puts "side-load" pressure on the ram, potentially snapping it or causing it to slip.

The "Right Tool" Solution: A Floor Jack

For a Malibu, you really want a 3-ton Low-Profile Floor Jack.

  • Low Entry: It can slide under the car even if you have a flat tire.
  • High Reach: Most have a lifting range from about 3 inches up to 18–20 inches.
  • Stability: The long chassis and wide wheels make it nearly impossible to tip over.

If You Must Use What You Have (The Safe Way)

If buying a new jack isn't in the cards today, do not put anything under the jack. Instead, do this:

  1. Use Ramps to Start: Use those automotive ramps I mentioned earlier. Drive the back wheels up onto them. This gives you the initial 6–8 inches of "pre-lift."
  2. The Jack as a Secondary: Now that the car is already high, your bottle jack will easily reach the frame. You can use it to lift the car just an inch or two higher off the ramps if you need to take a wheel off, but immediately swap in a jack stand.
  3. Solid Wood Only: If you absolutely must bridge a gap between the jack and the car, use a single, solid piece of 2x4 or 4x4 pressure-treated lumber on the top of the jack (the saddle). Never use bricks, stones, or plywood scraps, which can compress or shatter.

Where to Lift a Malibu

Since the Malibu is a "unibody" car, you can't just jack it up anywhere. Look for the pinch welds—that reinforced metal lip running along the side of the car under the doors. There are usually notches near the wheel wells indicating the safe spot.

Pro Tip: If you use a bottle jack on a pinch weld, it will likely bend the metal. You can buy a "pinch weld adapter" (a little rubber puck with a groove) for about $10 that fits on top of your jack to protect the car.

Moving to ramps is absolutely the right call. It is infinitely safer than the bottle jack and much easier for a long job like a hitch installation.

The $100+ ramps you saw at Harbor Freight were likely their heavy-duty solid steel or long aluminum trailer ramps. For a Chevy Malibu, you do not need those. High-impact resin ramps are the standard for home mechanics, and they easily fall under your budget.

I recommend the Hopkins Rhino Ramps 12,000 lb Capacity. You can find them at most major auto parts stores or big-box retailers for right around $76.

  • Strong and Reliable: They are rated to hold 12,000 lbs, which is more than enough for your Malibu. They have a 4.4-star rating from over 1,900 reviews, with users specifically noting their rugged construction and safety compared to jacks.
  • Smart Design: They feature integrated Core-Trac non-skid feet to prevent them from shooting forward as you drive up. They also have chamfered edges, which allows low-profile cars to drive on without scraping the bumper.
  • Space-Saving: They have a nestable design, meaning one stacks inside the other to save space in your garage when you are done.

Since you will be under the car for a while bolting up that hitch, would you like me to pull together some options for a comfortable mechanic's creeper and a set of solid rubber wheel chocks to complete your safety setup?

turns.prompt_text: What material is used in these ramps? I wonder.
turns.response_html:
The Hopkins Rhino Ramps (Model 11909) are made from a heavy-duty structural foam plastic, often specifically referred to as polypropylene resin.

While "plastic" might sound less sturdy than metal, in this application, it's actually an advantage for a few reasons:

  • Weight Distribution: The patented polymer internal support system (the grid-like pattern underneath) is designed to distribute the weight evenly, giving them that massive 12,000 lb capacity.
  • Flexibility: Unlike metal ramps which can dent or permanently bend if overloaded or struck, the resin has a slight bit of give that prevents it from snapping under normal load conditions.
  • Durability: They won't rust like steel or corrode like aluminum if they get wet or covered in garage chemicals.
  • Weight: They only weigh about 16 to 17 pounds for the pair, making them very easy to move around and stack compared to heavy steel ramps.

It's essentially the same type of high-impact resin used in heavy-duty toolboxes and industrial storage—tough, lightweight, and completely weather-proof.

turns.prompt_text: I already own a wheel chock it is nice to have another thing I was thinking was what I just be able to do even more cheaply, buy some 2x6s and 2x4s and make some trusses and create maybe a longer ramp to my ideal needs.
turns.response_html:
Building your own ramps out of lumber is a tried-and-true method in the car community. It’s often referred to as "cribbing" or "stepped ramps." Since you’re looking to customize the length and height for your Malibu’s specific clearance, this is a very viable path—but how you build them is the difference between a safe tool and a dangerous one.

1. Solid Stack vs. Truss Design

While you mentioned "trusses," you generally want to avoid a hollow truss design for car ramps.

  • Why: A truss relies entirely on the strength of your fasteners (screws/bolts) and the joints. If a joint fails or the wood splits at a screw point, the structure collapses instantly.
  • The Better Way: A Solid Stepped Design. This involves layering the boards flat on top of each other. This way, the weight of the car is transferred through the compressive strength of the wood grain directly to the ground.

2. Construction Plan: The "Stepped" Ramp

For a Malibu, which has a relatively low front and rear overhang, a longer, gradual ramp is great. Here is how to build a solid pair:

  • Materials: Use untreated 2x10s or 2x12s if possible (for a wider footprint), though 2x6s can work if you are very precise with your tire alignment.
  • The Layers:
    • Bottom layer: 4 feet long.
    • Second layer: 3 feet long.
    • Third layer: 2 feet long.
    • Top layer: 1 foot long.
  • The Stop: Screw a "stop block" (a vertical piece of 2x4) to the very end of the top layer so you can feel when you’ve reached the peak.
  • Fastening: Use heavy-duty construction adhesive (like Liquid Nails) between every layer and drive 3" deck screws every 6 inches. This makes the ramp behave like one solid beam of wood.

3. The Cost Reality

Before you head to the lumber yard, do a quick "back of the napkin" math check.

  • Lumber: To build a pair of 4-layer solid ramps using 2x10s, you’ll need about three or four 8-foot boards. Depending on current prices in Iowa, that’s roughly $45–$60.
  • Supplies: A box of screws and a tube of construction adhesive will add another $15–$20.
  • Total: You’re looking at $60–$80.

As you can see, you might only save about $10–$15 compared to the

, and the wood versions will be significantly heavier and harder to store. However, the wood ramps will be much longer and more stable for a low-clearance car.

Critical Safety Tips for Wood Ramps

  • Avoid "End-Grain" Loading: Never stand the wood on its end to get height; always stack it flat.
  • Bevel the Edges: Use a saw to cut a $45^\circ$ angle at the start of each "step." This makes the transition smoother for the tire and prevents the car from "kicking" the ramp forward as you try to climb it.
  • Watch for Splitting: Since you'll be driving screws into the ends of the boards, pre-drill your holes. This prevents the wood from splitting, which could compromise the integrity of the stack.
  • Grain Direction: When stacking, try to alternate the "cup" of the wood grain (the rings) between layers to prevent the whole ramp from warping over time.

turns.prompt_text: Would it possibly be a good idea to Lincoln Log or like every other change the direction of the of the lumber? So some pieces would be long and others would be pretty short.
turns.response_html:
The "Lincoln Log" approach you’re describing is a professional technique known as cribbing. It is widely used by firefighters, industrial movers, and heavy-duty mechanics because it is arguably the most stable way to support a static load.

However, there is a fundamental difference between a ramp (for driving up) and a crib (for sitting on). Here is how to evaluate that for your Malibu:

The Mechanics of Cribbing

In a cribbing setup, you alternate the direction of each layer by $90^\circ$. This creates a "box" or "tower" structure.

  • The Strength Point: The load-bearing capacity isn't actually the whole board; it’s the intersection points (the corners) where the wood overlaps.
  • Compression: Wood is incredibly strong in compression perpendicular to the grain. As long as the tiers are perfectly vertical and the corners are aligned, a simple $2 \times 4$ crib can hold tens of thousands of pounds.

Why Cribbing is Great for Maintenance

If you are adding a trailer hitch and the car will be up for a long time, cribbing is superior to jack stands for a few reasons:

  1. Surface Area: Unlike the tiny "head" of a jack stand, a crib supports the tire's entire footprint.
  2. No Tip-Over: A crib has a very wide base-to-height ratio. It is nearly impossible to knock a car off a properly built crib.
  3. Height Customization: You can keep adding layers until you reach your ideal working height.

The Problem: You Can't Drive Up It

The "Lincoln Log" style is generally for static support.

  • You cannot easily "drive up" an alternating stack because the tires would hit the cross-beams that are perpendicular to the direction of travel.
  • To use cribs, you would need to use a jack to lift the car, slide the crib under the tire, and then lower the car onto it. Since your bottle jack doesn't reach the car, you'd be back at square one.

The Hybrid Solution: "The Stepped Ramp"

If you want the stability of a wood stack but the convenience of driving up, the Solid Stepped Stack is your winner.

FeatureSolid Stepped StackAlternating Crib (Lincoln Log)
FunctionDrive-on RampStatic Support Block
ConstructionBoards stacked flat, same directionLayers at $90^\circ$ angles
HeightFixed once builtAdjustable/Modular
Malibu Use CaseBest for getting it up thereBest for holding it once it's up

Pro-Tip for your Malibu

Since the Malibu is front-wheel drive, if you are jacking up the back end, your front wheels (the ones with the parking brake and "Park" gear) are on the ground.

If you decide to build a Solid Stepped Ramp, make sure the top platform is long enough so the tire isn't "perched" on the edge. A standard tire footprint is about $6–9$ inches; I’d recommend a top platform of at least 12 to 15 inches to give yourself a safety margin.

One final woodwork tip: If you build these, avoid using pressure-treated wood if you plan to store them inside. The chemicals can off-gas, and the wood is often "wet" from the factory, which makes it prone to warping as it dries. Plain kiln-dried Douglas Fir or Pine from the local yard is cheaper and structurally excellent for this.

turns.prompt_text: I guess what I'm thinking is not that it's more of the earlier ramp but every other layer is kind of like Lincoln Logs or like a Genghis attack. So the first one would be the 10 inch board and it would be like 4 ft the second layer. Would it be 3 ft, but it would be, it would be like three or four different 10-in rotated 90° sections. And then, the third layer would be another, a 2-ft 10-in, width, and 1/4 layer. If there was a fourth layer would again be rotated. 90°
turns.response_html:
I see where your head is at—using a "cross-laminated" or "Jenga-style" approach to increase structural rigidity. In theory, alternating grain direction (like plywood) makes a structure very resistant to warping.

However, when it comes to drive-on ramps, there are two mechanical reasons why you should stick to a solid longitudinal stack (all boards facing the same way) rather than alternating them 90 degrees.

1. The "Thump" and Traction Problem

When you drive a Malibu up a ramp, the tires need a consistent, smooth surface to maintain grip.

  • The Issue: If every other layer is made of perpendicular 10-inch segments, your tires aren't driving on a flat plane; they are driving over a series of "ridges."
  • The Risk: As the tire hits each perpendicular board, the car will "thump." This causes the car to lurch slightly. If you give it too much gas to get over a ridge, you risk overshooting the ramp entirely. If you give it too little, the tire might spin, which can kick those perpendicular boards right out from under the stack like a projectile.

2. Shear Stress vs. Compression

A car driving up a ramp doesn't just exert downward weight; it exerts horizontal force (torque).

  • Longitudinal Boards: When all boards run the same way as the car, the tire's force is distributed along the entire length of the wood. The screws are just there to keep the boards from sliding.
  • Rotated Boards: If the top layer is rotated 90 degrees (running side-to-side), the tire's forward momentum is trying to "peel" those short boards off the layer below. You are relying entirely on the shear strength of your screws to keep the ramp from falling apart. Screws are great for holding things together, but they are not designed to be the primary structural defense against a 3,000-lb car’s torque.

A Safer "Heavy-Duty" DIY Design

If you want to build something that feels as "overbuilt" as a Lincoln Log structure but remains safe to drive on, I recommend a Solid Stack with Lateral Supports.

To get that "Lincoln Log" strength safely:

  1. The "Saddle" Sides: Instead of rotating the layers the tires touch, screw 2x4s along the sides of your main stack. This creates a "cradle" that prevents the boards from ever shifting sideways and gives you a visual guide so you don't drive off the edge.
  2. The Stop Block: Use a chunky 4x4 block at the very end of the top layer, bolted through multiple layers.
  3. Adhesive is Key: Use a generous amount of subfloor adhesive (like Loctite PL Premium) between the layers. This creates a "chemical weld" that is actually stronger than the wood itself, making the whole ramp act like one solid 6-inch thick timber.

A Note on Cost

Check the price of 2x10x8' boards at your local yard before you start. To build two of these ramps (4 layers high), you'll need about three 8-foot boards. In many places, that's $45–$50 alone. By the time you buy a box of structural screws and adhesive, you might be right back at the $70–$80 mark—very close to the price of the

.

If you have the wood lying around, the DIY route is great. If you have to buy it all new, the commercial ramps might actually be the cheaper (and lighter) option.

turns.prompt_text: Is there any specific kind of wood? I should use that. Would be both durable for this I guess, strong for this and cost-effective. It depends on the source of where I get it. I'm sure.
turns.response_html:
For a project like this in the Midwest, you actually have some great, affordable options. Since you’re in Iowa, you’ll mostly see three types of lumber at places like Menards or Home Depot.

Here is the breakdown of what to look for based on strength, durability, and cost:

1. The Best Choice: Douglas Fir (DF)

If you can find it, Douglas Fir is the gold standard for DIY ramps.

  • Why: It has a very high "compressive strength parallel to grain," meaning it doesn't squish easily. It’s also quite stiff and less likely to warp over time.
  • Cost: Usually around $12–$15 for an 8-foot 2x10. It’s slightly more expensive than standard framing lumber but worth it for the peace of mind.

2. The Local Heavyweight: Southern Yellow Pine (SYP)

In our region, you’ll often find Southern Yellow Pine, especially if you're looking at pressure-treated wood.

  • Why: SYP is actually one of the densest and strongest softwoods available. It’s incredibly tough and holds screws better than almost any other softwood.
  • Cost: Very cost-effective, often $11–$14 per board.
  • Note: If you buy the "Pressure Treated" version (the greenish stuff), it will last forever against garage floor moisture, but it is often very "wet" from the store. It can be heavy and might leak some chemicals on your hands, so wear gloves.

3. The Budget Option: SPF (Spruce-Pine-Fir)

This is your "standard" construction lumber used for framing house walls.

  • Why: It is the most cost-effective option (~$11 per board).
  • The Trade-off: It is a "softer" wood. While it will technically hold the weight of a Malibu (which is around 3,200 lbs), the wood might "dent" or compress where the tire sits over time. If you use SPF, you definitely want to go with 2x10 or 2x12 width to spread that weight out as much as possible.

"Pro-Shopper" Tips for the Lumber Yard:

  • Avoid the "Crown": Sight down the edge of the board like you’re aiming a rifle. If the board curves like a rainbow, don't buy it. You want the flattest boards possible so your "Lincoln Log" layers sit flush.
  • Skip the Knots: Try to find boards with the fewest knots possible, especially on the edges. A large knot is a structural weak point where the wood can split under the pressure of the car.
  • Width Matters: I strongly recommend using 2x10s (9.25" actual width). A Malibu tire is usually about 8 inches wide. A 2x6 is only 5.5 inches wide—your tires would hang off the sides, which is a major safety hazard.

If you go with the Southern Yellow Pine (SYP), you'll get the best bang for your buck in terms of raw strength.

turns.prompt_text: Usually what I do is I pick some up and then maybe a week later, I'll actually get to it. And then figure out some issue I run into and I'll write it down and then I'll get to it a week or two later after that.
turns.response_html:
That "slow and steady" workflow is actually a superpower in the DIY world. It’s the best way to avoid the "Sunday night panic" when a 20-minute job suddenly turns into a 6-hour ordeal because of a snapped bolt or a missing tool.

Since you're planning to let the wood sit for a week and then spend some time troubleshooting, here are two specific "heads-ups" for your notebook that will save you a headache later.

1. The "Ames Humidity" Wood Rule

Since you’re in Iowa and it's mid-May, the humidity can jump around quite a bit. If you buy Southern Yellow Pine or Douglas Fir and just lean it against your garage wall for a week, it will likely "potato chip" (warp) by the time you go to build.

  • Store it Flat: Lay the boards flat on the garage floor, but put scraps of wood (stickers) underneath them so they aren't touching the concrete directly. Concrete holds moisture and will make one side of your board expand faster than the other.
  • Acclimation is Good: Letting the wood sit for a week is actually great—it allows the moisture levels to stabilize so your ramps don't pull themselves apart after you build them.

2. The Malibu "Hitch Hurdles"

When you get to your "write down the issues" phase for the Malibu hitch, look out for these three common sticking points:

  • The "Fishwire" Shuffle: Most Malibu hitches require you to "fish" bolts through a hole in the frame using a thin wire. It’s a bit like a game of Operation. Tip: Don't pull the wire off the bolt until the hitch is actually up and the nut is started—if you drop a bolt into the frame, that’s an hour you’ll never get back.
  • Heat Shield Surgery: You’ll likely have to trim the aluminum heat shields around your exhaust to make room for the hitch brackets. A pair of aviation shears (tin snips) makes this a 2-minute job; trying to do it with pliers is miserable.
  • Exhaust Drop: You’ll need to pop the exhaust out of its rubber hangers to get the hitch into position. Spray those rubber hangers with a little soapy water or WD-40 first, and they’ll slide right off.

If you don't already have one, do you have a torque wrench? Those hitch bolts usually need to be tightened to a specific spec (often around $60\text{ ft-lbs}$ or $45\text{ ft-lbs}$) to make sure they don't rattle loose while you're driving.
